Gather
GAþH-er
v.
Old English gaderian, “to gather, collect, assemble.” Renders the Hebrew qābats, “to gather, collect,” and ’āsaph, “to gather, take in”; and the Greek sunagō, “to lead together, gather,” and episunagō, “to gather together upon.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Gather is one of Scripture’s great divine verbs: the action by which God draws His scattered people to Himself, the harvester gathers the wheat into the barn, the shepherd gathers the lambs in his arms, and the King at the end of the age gathers His elect from the four winds. The Old Testament repeats the gathering promise to a scattered Israel: I will gather you from the people, and assemble you out of the countries where ye have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel. Christ takes the verb on His own lips with deepest affection at the Lord’s lament over Jerusalem: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!—a verse that lays bare both the tender persistence of Christ’s gathering will and the awful reality of the gathered ones’ refusal. He continues the theme in His Olivet discourse: and he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Paul speaks of the gathering together unto him (2 Thess 2:1) as a name for the church’s consummation in Christ’s presence. Beyond these decisive uses, the verb governs ordinary church life: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them; not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; the apostles gather the multitudes to hear the Word; the church gathers on the Lord’s day for worship. There is also a gathering of judgment: the tares are gathered first and bound in bundles to be burned, the chaff is gathered and burned, the kings of the earth are gathered to the battle of the great day of God Almighty. The verb therefore has its two faces: the gracious gathering of the elect to Christ for life, and the judicial gathering of the rebel for wrath. Both are God’s acts; both are inevitable; and which gathering one is gathered into is settled by the response of the heart to the present gathering call of the gospel: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines GATHER as to bring together; to collect; to assemble; to convene; to draw together from distant or remote places; to bring into one place or one body.

expand to see more

GATHER, v.t. — 1. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things into one place, or into one aggregate body. 2. To collect, as fruits; to pluck and pick up. 3. To bring into one body or interest; to associate. 4. To collect in abundance; to accumulate; to amass. 5. To assemble; to congregate; to convene. 6. To gain by induction or inference.

GATHERING, ppr. — Collecting; assembling; bringing together; drawing together.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 23:37 — "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!"

Matthew 24:31 — "And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."

Hebrews 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

2 Thessalonians 2:1 — "Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The gathering of God’s people is corrupted by the consumer-spirituality register that treats the Lord’s Day gathering as an optional amenity and by the streaming-church habit that has displaced the actual assembling with a screen-mediated facsimile—against Christ’s own tender will to gather and Hebrews 10’s plain command not to forsake the assembling.

expand to see more

The Lord’s Day gathering of God’s people is, in Scripture, a non-negotiable expression of the gathering Christ Himself accomplishes in His people—where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them; not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together. The consumer-spirituality register of contemporary evangelicalism has corrupted this by treating Sunday assembly as one option among many for the weekend—attended when convenient, skipped when inconvenient, chosen or abandoned by personal preference as one chooses a restaurant. The very tenderness of Christ’s lament over Jerusalem (how often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not) carries forward as the standing rebuke of every soul who refuses His present gathering call.

The streaming-church habit, born of necessity and now retained by preference, is a closely related corruption. The believer is ‘at church’ in front of a screen, watching a service from his couch, and counts himself gathered when Scripture knows nothing of the category. The gathering of the saints is by definition bodily co-presence: bodies in one place, voices in one room, bread broken among real hands, the laying-on of hands and the holy kiss and the looking each other in the eye—none of which a screen mediates. The streaming option has real and limited uses (the genuinely sick, the providentially hindered, the homebound saint) but it is not the gathering. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of the practice: the saint, like the saints of every age, gathered bodily with his local church on the Lord’s day, taking his ordinary place among the assembled people in whose midst Christ has promised to be.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qābats (to gather, collect) and ’āsaph (to gather, take in); Greek sunagō (to lead together) and episunagō (to gather together upon—Heb 10:25)—the divine gathering of the elect to Christ for life set against the judicial gathering of the rebel for wrath.

expand to see more

Hebrew qābats (H6908) — to gather, collect, assemble (the prophetic-promise verb of Israel’s ingathering).

Hebrew ’āsaph (H622) — to gather, take in (the harvest verb).

Greek sunagō (G4863) — to lead together, gather (root of synagogue).

Greek episunagō (G1996) / episunagōgē (G1997) — to gather together upon / the gathering (Heb 10:25; 2 Thess 2:1).

Usage

"Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them—the gathered church is the place of Christ’s promised presence."

"Christ’s tender will to gather is met, often, by His people’s refusal—how often would I have gathered... and ye would not."

"Streaming presence is not biblical gathering; the assembling Hebrews 10 commands is bodily co-presence among real saints."
